The National Association of Genealogical Services lists more than 700 forensic genealogists at its Web site.

DNA has become a mainstay in genealogy research, offering the ability to create family trees that may be lacking vital records or other information -- the reason why so many people get started in the hobby of genealogy is to learn more about their family history.
But just because a test reveals a match, that doesn't automatically confirm the family tree.
It's forensic genealogy that provides a link between the test results and the historical record.
Abrams, a resident of Manhattan Beach, Calif., is a member of the association, and the president of her company, Abrams & Associates (www.forensic genealogists.net).

It's a rare occurrence for a non-relative to hold this DNA.

Abrams worked on the case for about three months, interviewing the man, matching the handwriting sample to letters written by the woman's great-grandmother and comparing genealogical records to prove the man was a relative.
Another case in which Abrams was involved was that of a brother and sister who died.
The woman had died about 25 years ago, and her only sibling was a mentally challenged man who had never lived with her.
